pages.text: Early morning mist curled around the giant trees of Kakum National Park in Ghana’s Central Region. Nine-year-old Ama smiled proudly at her cousin Jayden, who was visiting from London for the very first time. ‘Welcome to our rainforest, Jayden!’ said Ama. ‘Wait until you see where we are walking today!’
sentences: Early morning mist curled around the giant trees of Kakum National Park in Ghana’s Central Region.
Nine-year-old Ama smiled proudly at her cousin Jayden, who was visiting from London for the very first time.
‘Welcome to our rainforest, Jayden!’ said Ama.
‘Wait until you see where we are walking today!’
pages.alt: Ama and her cousin Jayden stand at the lush green entrance of Kakum National Park with Ranger Kweku in the morning mist.

pages.text: At the visitor centre, Ranger Kweku pointed to a wooden map of the park. ‘Before we climb,’ he said, ‘every visitor learns the ecotourism rules. Keep every wrapper in your bag, stay on the marked trail, speak softly so we do not frighten wildlife, and never pick plants or feed the animals. A good visitor leaves only footprints!’
sentences: At the visitor centre, Ranger Kweku pointed to a wooden map of the park.
‘Before we climb,’ he said, ‘every visitor learns the ecotourism rules.
Keep every wrapper in your bag, stay on the marked trail, speak softly so we do not frighten wildlife, and never pick plants or feed the animals.
A good visitor leaves only footprints!’
pages.alt: Ranger Kweku points to a carved wooden trail map while Ama and Jayden tuck their water bottles into their backpacks.

pages.text: They hiked up the shaded forest steps until they reached the first wooden platform high in the trees. Stretching ahead of them hung the famous Kakum Canopy Walkway, seven suspension bridges made of strong ropes, cables and wooden planks, three hundred and fifty metres long in total!
sentences: They hiked up the shaded forest steps until they reached the first wooden platform high in the trees.
Stretching ahead of them hung the famous Kakum Canopy Walkway, seven suspension bridges made of strong ropes, cables and wooden planks, three hundred and fifty metres long in total!
pages.alt: Ama and Jayden look out at the rope-and-plank suspension bridge of the Kakum Canopy Walkway high among the green treetops.

pages.text: Jayden held the side ropes tightly as his sneakers stepped onto the first bridge. Forty metres below, the forest floor looked like a deep green carpet! ‘It sways a little!’ Jayden gasped. Ama held his hand and smiled. ‘Look at the thick steel cables and safety nets, Jayden. Step steadily in the middle of the planks, and look out at the treetops!’
sentences: Jayden held the side ropes tightly as his sneakers stepped onto the first bridge.

Ama held his hand and smiled.
‘Look at the thick steel cables and safety nets, Jayden.
Step steadily in the middle of the planks, and look out at the treetops!’
pages.alt: Ama encourages Jayden as they walk across the high rope-and-plank canopy bridge forty metres above the forest floor.

pages.text: On the third tree platform, Jayden forgot his fear and lifted his camera. Across the sunlit upper canopy, a yellow-casqued hornbill glided on wide dark wings, and two mona monkeys leaped from branch to branch. ‘Most rainforest animals live high up here in the canopy where flowers and fruits grow in the sunshine,’ whispered Ranger Kweku.
sentences: On the third tree platform, Jayden forgot his fear and lifted his camera.
Across the sunlit upper canopy, a yellow-casqued hornbill glided on wide dark wings, and two mona monkeys leaped from branch to branch.
‘Most rainforest animals live high up here in the canopy where flowers and fruits grow in the sunshine,’ whispered Ranger Kweku.
pages.alt: From the wooden platform high in an emergent tree, Jayden and Ama watch a hornbill and two monkeys in the sunlit branches.

pages.text: ‘Why did people build a walkway up in the trees instead of cutting a wide road through the forest?’ asked Jayden. ‘Because a road would cut down ancient trees and break the animals’ home apart,’ said Ranger Kweku. ‘The canopy walkway lets visitors experience the forest from above while leaving the ground and roots undisturbed below.’
sentences: ‘Why did people build a walkway up in the trees instead of cutting a wide road through the forest?’ asked Jayden.
‘Because a road would cut down ancient trees and break the animals’ home apart,’ said Ranger Kweku.
‘The canopy walkway lets visitors experience the forest from above while leaving the ground and roots undisturbed below.’
pages.alt: Ranger Kweku points down to the unbroken green forest floor far beneath the suspension bridge.

pages.text: ‘Even more importantly,’ Ranger Kweku continued, ‘Kakum protects the headwaters of the Kakum River and other streams that supply clean drinking water to Cape Coast and surrounding towns. The forest trees also absorb carbon dioxide and release fresh oxygen. Protecting these trees protects thousands of families!’
sentences: ‘Even more importantly,’ Ranger Kweku continued, ‘Kakum protects the headwaters of the Kakum River and other streams that supply clean drinking water to Cape Coast and surrounding towns.
The forest trees also absorb carbon dioxide and release fresh oxygen.
Protecting these trees protects thousands of families!’
pages.alt: A clear forest stream sparkles among mossy rocks and giant buttress roots on the floor of Kakum National Park.

pages.text: ‘How does our ticket help the forest?’ asked Ama. ‘That is the heart of ecotourism,’ said Ranger Kweku. ‘When visitors pay entrance fees, hire trained local guides, and buy crafts or food from nearby villages, the community earns income from keeping the forest standing rather than cutting trees for timber or hunting wild animals.’
sentences: ‘How does our ticket help the forest?’ asked Ama.
‘That is the heart of ecotourism,’ said Ranger Kweku.

‘When visitors pay entrance fees, hire trained local guides, and buy crafts or food from nearby villages, the community earns income from keeping the forest standing rather than cutting trees for timber or hunting wild animals.’
pages.alt: Near the park craft stalls, visitors buy woven baskets and cocoa snacks from smiling local community vendors.

pages.text: Back on the ground trail, Jayden spotted a plastic bottle someone had dropped near a fern. Before Ranger Kweku could bend down, Jayden picked it up and placed it in the recycling bin at the trailhead. ‘Wait, Ranger Kweku,’ Jayden asked, ‘is Kakum a UNESCO World Heritage Site like Cape Coast Castle?’ ‘Cape Coast Castle is an inscribed World Heritage Site,’ explained Ranger Kweku, ‘and Kakum is on Ghana’s UNESCO Tentative List as a national treasure we must keep protecting!’

pages.alt: Jayden places a stray plastic bottle into a bin at the trailhead while Ama and Ranger Kweku smile approvingly.

pages.text: As they rode back toward Cape Coast in the afternoon sunshine, Jayden looked through his photos of giant trees and hornbills. ‘In London, I will show my class that Ghana’s rainforest is a living treasure,’ he said. Ama beamed. ‘And we will keep guarding it from the roots to the treetops!’ The end.

pages.alt: Ama and Jayden sit together looking at rainforest photos on Jayden’s camera with the green hills of Kakum behind them.

activities.question: Which of these is one of the responsible ecotourism rules Ranger Kweku taught at Kakum?
options: Keep all litter in your bag, stay on the trail and speak softly
Pick wildflowers and feed snacks to the monkeys
Shout loudly so birds fly out of the trees
Carve your name into the bark of ancient trees
activities.explanation: Responsible visitors leave no litter, stay on marked trails, speak quietly, and never disturb plants or wildlife.

activities.question: Besides protecting wildlife, how does Kakum National Park help families in Cape Coast and nearby towns?
options: It protects the forest streams that supply clean drinking water
It sends ocean waves up to the hilltops
It makes plastic bottles out of tree leaves
It keeps the sun from shining in the daytime
activities.explanation: Kakum protects the watershed of the Kakum River and streams that provide fresh drinking water to Cape Coast and surrounding communities.

activities.definition: Responsible travel to natural areas that conserves the environment and supports local communities.
distractors: Cutting down forests to build large factories
Keeping wild animals locked in small cages at home

activities.question: How does ecotourism help protect the trees and animals of Kakum?
options: Ticket fees and guide jobs help locals earn income keeping trees safe
Visitors bring axes to cut down the tallest trees
Tourists take wild monkeys home on aeroplanes
Rangers pave the whole forest floor with concrete
activities.explanation: Ecotourism funds park rangers and creates local jobs so protecting the living forest benefits everyone.

activities.prompt: What would happen to the animals and the Kakum River if people cut down the trees around the stream headwaters?
Put Ama and Jayden’s Kakum adventure in order.
items: Ranger Kweku teaches the ecotourism rules at the visitor centre.
Ama helps Jayden walk bravely across the high canopy bridge.
They spot a hornbill and monkeys in the sunlit upper canopy.
Jayden picks up a stray plastic bottle to keep the trail clean.

activities.prompt: How did Ama help Jayden when he felt nervous on the first high bridge, and how did Jayden feel afterwards?

glossary.definition: Careful travel to natural places that protects wildlife and helps local communities.
The high, leafy roof formed by the tops of tall rainforest trees.
The small streams where a river begins.
Something very valuable and precious that must be protected.
